figure: Figure 14.1 (Select models: screen on capability, then benchmark on the workload)
evidence: The orange box under 'Candidate models' reads 'Capability' / 'MMU/GSM8K'. The standard LLM capability benchmark is MMLU; 'MMU' is not a recognized LLM capability test and collides with 'memory-management unit'. Neither the in-figure note nor the caption defines 'MMU', so the label is unexplained and is almost certainly a dropped 'L'.
acceptance_test: The orange box reads 'MMLU/GSM8K' and the benchmark name matches whatever the section-14 body text calls the capability screen (verify the body uses MMLU; if the body also says MMU, correct both to MMLU).

figure: Figure 15.1 (FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic) - BEFORE panel
issue: BEFORE annotation is internally inconsistent: it labels the traffic O(L^2) but then lists 'every query re-reads the K/V rows', which is O(L^2 d), and is not the dominant cost of the labeled 'materialized' naive kernel.
evidence: BEFORE caption line: 'O(L^2) HBM traffic: L x L intermediate written + every query re-reads the K/V rows'. A per-query re-read of all K/V rows costs O(L^2 d), not O(L^2); the O(L^2) term is the L x L S-matrix write+read. Section 15.3 prose (printed 250) correctly attributes the O(L^2) to the materialized L x L intermediate ('a naive kernel writes the L x L attention matrix to HBM and reads it back, so the materialized intermediate itself is O(L^2)') and does NOT include the per-query K/V re-read clause, so the figure added an inconsistent clause.
acceptance_test: Reword the BEFORE annotation so the O(L^2) is attributed solely to the L x L S-matrix round-trip (e.g. 'O(L^2) HBM traffic: the L x L S matrix is written to and read back from HBM; Q/K/V are O(L d), lower order'), or, if a per-query K/V re-stream is intended, label it as the non-fused tiled case with its own O(L^2 d) term. The result must match the section 15.3 prose.

figure: Figure 13.1 (The reference-architecture escalation ladder) - blue de-escalation arrow
issue: The figure's de-escalation trigger set (privacy, sovereignty, on-device, cost) is disjoint from section 13.2's de-escalation definition (the reverse of the performance climb: low utilization, SLO headroom), so the same term denotes two different trigger sets across the figure and the prose.
evidence: Fig 13.1 blue label: 'DE-ESCALATE: privacy . sovereignty . on-device . cost (primary triggers)'; caption: 'de-escalation (blue) fires on privacy, sovereignty, on-device requirements, or cost.' Section 13.2 prose (printed 226): 'De-escalation is the same discipline in reverse. A workload drops a tier when the constraint that justified the climb has measurably gone away: sustained low utilization (e.g. 30-day p95 utilization < 40%), SLO headroom >= 2x (30-day p95 TTFT <= half the SLO) ...'. The prose's triggers (utilization, SLO headroom) do not appear in the figure, and the figure's triggers (privacy, etc.) do not appear in the visible prose.
acceptance_test: Reconcile: either add the performance-based de-escalation (low utilization / SLO headroom) to the figure's blue label as a co-equal trigger group, or explicitly distinguish in section 13.2 between (i) performance de-escalation (reverse of the red triggers) and (ii) non-performance de-escalation (privacy/sovereignty/on-device/cost) and cross-reference the figure. After the change a reader should see one consistent definition of 'de-escalation' across figure and prose.

evidence: In-plot note: '...then survivors are measured on the real workload against the SLO gate.' Caption: 'the deployment benchmark (which system meets our SLO)'. Diagram: orange box under 'Survivors' = 'Deploy bench (goodput)'; orange box under 'Selection' = 'TCO + SLO gate'.
